text:
About the RMMT Fellowship
Welcome to the RMMT Fellowship Curriculum Pack.
Use the sidebar to move through the RMMT Fellowship information, curriculum overview, module guides, supporting tools, MEL, scale-up, and facilitator guidance.
Teaching materials and exercise templates will be available in the accompanying RMMT Fellowship GitHub repository.
The Regional Malaria Modelling Translational (RMMT) Fellowship is a six-month executive programme designed to strengthen the use of modelling in malaria decision-making. Delivered from May to October 2025, the inaugural Fellowship brought together 21 fellows from seven countries—Angola, Eswatini, Ghana, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, and Zambia—nominated by their National Malaria Programmes (NMPs). The programme was implemented by the Modelling and Simulation Hub, Africa (MASHA) at the University of Cape Town, in partnership with the Southern African Development Community (SADC) Malaria Elimination 8 Initiative (E8) and the Clinton Health Access Initiative (CHAI) South Africa Office, and funded by the Gates Foundation (GF). The Fellowship addresses a critical gap between modelling evidence and its use in policy and programme decision-making. It builds the capacity of policymakers, programme leaders, and technical staff to interpret model-based insights as a practical decision-support tool in resource-constrained settings.
The Fellowship combined in-person and virtual learning across key areas, with three immersive, full-time in-person blocks held in May, August, and October 2025. The curriculum topics spanned the full modelling process—from framing policy-relevant questions and understanding systems, through model design, development, and critique, to interpreting outputs and communicating findings—while also addressing cross-cutting themes such as uncertainty, health economics, and stakeholder engagement. A central component was the Capstone Project, where fellows worked in country teams to develop proposals for modelling analyses to address priority policy questions.
The RMMT Fellowship demonstrated strong early impact, including increased confidence in interpreting modelling outputs, strengthened collaboration between technical and policy stakeholders, and a pipeline of country-led modelling projects aligned with programme priorities. Fellows also reported substantial gains in their ability to apply model-based insights in decision-making processes, define policy-relevant questions, and translate findings into actionable recommendations. The inaugural implementation of the RMMT Fellowship has demonstrated its ability to strengthen capacity to bridge the gap between modelling and policy, supporting more informed, data-driven decision-making in malaria programmes. It also provides a framework that can be readily transferred to other areas of disease modelling for public health.

title: RMMT Fellowship Curriculum Pack
text:
Purpose of the Curriculum Pack
This curriculum pack has been developed to document and consolidate the content, structure, and learning approach of the RMMT Fellowship, providing a practical resource for future delivery, adaptation, and scale-up. It is intended to support facilitators, partners, and institutions in implementing similar programmes, as well as to enable broader access to the Fellowship’s materials and methodologies.
The pack is organised to provide both a high-level overview of the curriculum framework and detailed guidance for delivery at the module level. It includes descriptions of core themes, session structures, learning objectives, and practical exercises, alongside tools, templates, and resources to support application in real-world contexts. In doing so, it aims to ensure that the curriculum is not only informative but also actionable, enabling users to replicate and adapt the Fellowship to different settings and priority areas.

The Challenge
Malaria in Africa continues to be of great public health concern despite significant progress in recent years. To effectively address the malaria burden and achieve the goal of elimination, it is imperative to have robust, evidence-based strategies and policies. Disease modelling plays a crucial role in informing decision-making by providing insights into disease transmission and dynamics, evaluating the impact of different interventions, and identifying optimal strategies for malaria control and elimination.

Malaria Modelling and Analytics: Leaders in Africa
The Regional Malaria Modelling Translational (RMMT) Fellowship is part of the Malaria Modelling and Analytics: Leaders in Africa (MMALA) programme. MMALA seeks to develop a critical mass of African malaria modellers to meet the need for tailored quantitative malaria decision support in a sustainable way. It provides a nexus for the training and career development of local individuals who will be able to address the needs of their National Malaria Programmes (NMPs) to shape strategic plans, secure necessary funds, and evaluate and improve the impact of control programmes.
MMALA achieves this by building capacity in malaria modelling and working with strategic partners to increase the uptake of modelling in decision-making; facilitating the sharing of expertise among modellers in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA); providing holistic skills through training and active mentorship; and building an enabling environment to improve modellers’ access to timely, high-quality data. A highly skilled cohort of African modellers, working in an enabling environment, facilitated by strategic partners, alongside NMPs who have developed the appetite and literacy for incorporating modelling approaches in strategic planning will culminate from this project.

Regional Malaria Modelling Translational Fellowship
The RMMT Fellowship is an accredited, six-month executive fellowship programme targeted at building modelling translational capacity in Africa. Led by the Modelling and Simulation Hub, Africa (MASHA) at the University of Cape Town (UCT) in partnership with the Southern African Development Community (SADC) Malaria Elimination 8 Initiative (E8), and the Clinton Health Access Initiative (CHAI) South Africa Office, funded by the Gates Foundation, the fellowship targets key decision-makers, policymakers and implementers within the public sector working across various levels in health management. The inaugural RMMT Fellowship cohort consisted of 21 fellows from seven countries: Angola, Eswatini, Ghana, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, and Zambia.

The RMMT fellowship focuses on bridging the gap between technical modelling outputs and actionable policy strategies to advance malaria control and elimination efforts.

The inaugural RMMT Fellowship was held May to October 2025, in a hybrid format with three immersive in-person weeks and virtual sessions in between. Throughout the programme, fellows worked in country teams towards a Capstone Project, which was to develop a modelling project on a policy topic of priority for their country.

title: RMMT Fellowship
text:
Fellowship Structure and Delivery Approach
The RMMT Fellowship is designed as a structured, six-month executive programme that combines conceptual understanding with practical application. Participants engage with modelling through a sequence of learning activities that progressively build confidence and capability, supported by opportunities to apply learning to real-world programme challenges.
The Fellowship is delivered through a hybrid structure to maximise contact time while fitting in with the demands of fellows’ work schedules. There are three immersive, full-time in-person blocks, with virtual sessions held twice a month in between the immersive week blocks.
A range of teaching methods is employed to support adult learning and practical application. These include lectures to introduce key concepts, facilitated discussions to draw on participant experience, and interactive and group-based exercises to apply learning to real-world scenarios. The programme also emphasises peer learning, mentorship, and engagement with external experts, fostering collaboration and strengthening the link between technical knowledge and policy application.
A central component of the programme is the Capstone Project, where fellows work in country teams to develop modelling-focused proposals addressing priority policy questions. This applied element ensures that learning is directly linked to programme needs and supports the translation of knowledge into practice.

title: RMMT Fellowship
text:
Target Audience and Participant Profile
The Fellowship is targeted at professionals working within National Malaria Programmes (NMPs), Ministries of Health, and partner organisations who are involved in policy development, programme implementation, and data-driven decision-making. Participants are typically nominated by their respective countries and represent a diverse range of roles, including programme managers, monitoring and evaluation specialists, surveillance officers, data analysts, and policy advisors.
This diversity is intentional, reflecting the need for cross-functional engagement to effectively translate modelling into practice. Participants bring a combination of technical expertise and practical experience, ensuring that learning is grounded in real-world programme contexts and that modelling approaches are aligned with operational needs.

title: Curriculum Overview
text:
Overview of Core Themes
The RMMT Fellowship curriculum is structured around a set of interconnected themes that reflect the full lifecycle of modelling for policy and programme decision-making. These themes span from foundational concepts—such as understanding what modelling is, systems thinking, and the model building process—through to applied components including model design, scenario analysis, and interpretation of outputs. Cross-cutting areas such as uncertainty, health economics, subnational tailoring, and stakeholder engagement are integrated throughout to ensure relevance to real-world contexts.
The content is designed to provide participants with both the conceptual understanding and practical tools required to engage critically with modelling and to use model-based insights effectively within programme and policy contexts. The curriculum also places strong emphasis on critical engagement with models, including questioning assumptions, interpreting limitations, and effectively communicating findings to diverse audiences. Together, these themes provide a comprehensive foundation for understanding, applying, and using modelling to inform malaria programmes.

title: Curriculum Overview
text:
How the Modules Fit Together
The modules are designed to build progressively, supporting a structured learning journey from foundational knowledge to applied practice. Early modules introduce key concepts and frameworks, establishing a shared understanding of modelling and its role within complex health systems. This is followed by modules focused on the modelling process itself, including question formulation, model design, and stakeholder roles, which equip participants with the tools to engage in or commission modelling work. Subsequent modules emphasise interpretation, critique, and application, enabling fellows to analyse outputs, assess uncertainty, and translate findings into actionable insights. The curriculum includes applied exercises throughout and culminates in a capstone project, where participants integrate learning across modules to address real-world programme questions. This progression ensures that learning is cumulative, practical, and directly relevant to participants’ roles.

title: Curriculum Overview
text:
Competency Areas and Expected Outcomes
The curriculum is aligned with three core competency areas: 1) understanding and interpreting modelling outputs; 2) applying modelling to decision-making; and 3) communication, collaboration, and influence. Across these domains, participants are expected to develop both technical literacy and practical skills.





By the end of the Fellowship, fellows should be able to critically interpret model outputs, including assumptions and uncertainty; define and refine policy-relevant modelling questions; and apply modelling insights to inform strategic planning and resource allocation. In addition, participants are expected to strengthen their ability to communicate complex technical information to non-technical audiences, facilitate dialogue between modellers and decision-makers, and advocate for the use of evidence in policy and programme contexts.

title: Curriculum Overview
section: Alignment with Policy and Programme Needs
text:
Alignment with Policy and Programme Needs
The curriculum is intentionally designed to align with the needs of policymakers and programme implementers, rather than focusing solely on technical modelling skills. Content is grounded in real-world malaria programme challenges, including intervention prioritisation, resource allocation, and subnational tailoring. Emphasis is placed on ensuring that modelling is used to address relevant and actionable questions, and that outputs are translated into formats that support decision-making. The curriculum also reflects the realities of constrained resources, data limitations, and competing priorities within health systems. By integrating technical knowledge with policy application, the Fellowship aims to bridge the gap between modelling and practice, strengthening the capacity of participants to use evidence effectively within their institutional contexts.

title: Curriculum Overview
text:
Approach to Learning
The RMMT Fellowship is designed as a practical, participant-centred learning programme. Its aim is not only to introduce modelling concepts, but to support fellows to apply modelling, evidence synthesis, and technical–policy dialogue to real malaria programme decisions.
The curriculum recognises that fellows bring different types of expertise. Some participants may have experience in malaria programme implementation, surveillance, monitoring and evaluation, or policy development, while others may have more technical or analytical backgrounds. The learning approach therefore values both technical knowledge and programme experience. Modelling is presented as a collaborative process that depends on clear questions, contextual understanding, appropriate data, transparent assumptions, and effective communication.






NoteLearning Principle



The Fellowship treats participants as active contributors to the learning process. Country experience, programme knowledge, and policy insight are used as core learning resources throughout the curriculum.


Learning activities are designed to help fellows move between concepts, application, and reflection. Modules combine short technical inputs with facilitated discussion, practical exercises, country team work, and opportunities to connect learning to capstone projects. This structure allows fellows to test ideas, question assumptions, and consider how modelling can support decision-making in their own contexts.

A key feature of the Fellowship is the emphasis on learning across disciplines. Fellows are encouraged to consider both technical and decision-making perspectives: what a model can estimate, what assumptions shape the results, how uncertainty should be interpreted, and what decision the evidence is intended to inform. This helps ensure that modelling is understood not as a purely technical exercise, but as part of a broader process of strategic planning, implementation, and policy dialogue.






TipConnecting Technical and Policy Perspectives



Throughout the curriculum, fellows are encouraged to ask: What decision could this analysis inform? What assumptions should decision-makers understand? What uncertainties remain? How can findings be communicated clearly and responsibly?


The learning approach also recognises that uncertainty is central to both modelling and public health decision-making. Rather than treating uncertainty as a weakness, the curriculum uses it as an opportunity to discuss confidence, risk, data limitations, and alternative scenarios. Fellows are supported to interpret uncertainty in ways that are meaningful for programme planning and policy decisions.
The Fellowship uses an iterative learning model. Ideas introduced in early modules are revisited and strengthened through later sessions, practical exercises, and capstone project work. Fellows gradually build from understanding modelling concepts to formulating policy-relevant questions, interpreting outputs, communicating findings, and considering how modelling evidence can be embedded in programme decision-making.

title: Capstone Projects
text:
Overview
A central component of the RMMT Fellowship is the Capstone Project, through which fellows apply the knowledge and skills acquired during the programme to real-world policy challenges. Working collaboratively in country teams, the aim of the Capstone Projects is for fellows to identify and develop modelling-focused projects addressing high-priority malaria policy and implementation questions relevant to their national contexts.
Each Capstone Project should focus on a high-impact, policy-relevant question aligned with national malaria priorities. The process emphasises the practical application of modelling to inform intervention design, optimise resource allocation, and accelerate progress toward malaria control and elimination goals.
Collectively, the Capstone Projects demonstrate the value of embedding modelling within decision-making processes. They highlight how locally led, policy-driven analyses can generate actionable insights to guide programme planning, improve allocative efficiency, and support evidence-based advocacy for sustained investment in malaria programmes.

title: Capstone Projects
text:
Delivery Approach

Project Structure
Througout the course of the Fellowship, country teams develop structured proposals that integrated epidemiological and economic perspectives, including: a clearly defined policy problem, key modelling questions, required data inputs, priority outcomes, and scenario-based analyses of alternative intervention strategies. Proposals also incorporate economic evaluations to assess affordability and cost-effectiveness, alongside implementation considerations through Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, and Threats (SWOT) analyses and defined next steps for policy uptake.







Capstone Presentations
During the final week of the Fellowship, country teams present their Capstone Project proposals to the full cohort as well as to invited representatives from Ministries of Health and National Malaria Programmes (NMPs), who may join virtually or in person. These presentations serve as a critical platform for fellows to demonstrate the knowledge and skills gained throughout the programme, particularly their ability to translate modelling concepts into clear, policy-relevant recommendations. Importantly, engagement with key national stakeholders helps to validate the relevance of the proposed analyses, build buy-in, and highlight the practical value of modelling in informing programme decisions. This interaction is also an opportunity to lay the groundwork for continued collaboration and positioned the projects as a foundation for future modelling work within NMPs.


Group Work Sessions
Throughout the Fellowship, we recommend allocating time for fellows to work in their Capstone Project groups as well as opportunities to present and receive feedback at key stages in the project development. This can be done through a mix of sessions during the in-person blocks (especially Block 2) and virtual sessions. Presenting interim work allows for constructive feedback on the application of the Fellowship topics and shared learning across the cohort.

For each audience, what is the ideal approach (e.g. format, duration, setting, practicalities/formalities involved)?
How valuable do you think each format is for each audience (low, medium, high)?
What practical considerations should be taken into account?

Discussion Questions for Engaging with Modellers:

At what stage of the decision-making cycle would you prefer to engage with modellers (problem definition, data collection, model building, interpretation, dissemination)?
How often would you like to interact with the modelling team (one-off workshop, regular briefings, embedded collaboration)?
What formats of engagement do you find most effective — technical workshops, short policy dialogues, dashboards, written briefs, or joint scenario discussions?
Would you prefer that models are co-developed (you contribute to assumptions and scenarios) or mainly reviewed once results are ready?

How can you build local capacity during this process?

Reinforce that communication should focus on decisions and implications

title: Facilitator Guidance
text:
Preparing to Deliver the Fellowship
Successful delivery of the RMMT Fellowship depends on thoughtful preparation, contextual awareness, and a commitment to participant-centred learning. Facilitators should view preparation as more than reviewing slides and materials; it involves understanding the participants, their programme contexts, and the policy challenges they are seeking to address.
Before delivery, facilitators should familiarise themselves with the overall Fellowship learning journey and the relationship between individual modules, capstone projects, and programme objectives. Particular attention should be paid to the backgrounds and responsibilities of participants, as the Fellowship cohort typically includes policymakers, programme managers, surveillance officers, monitoring and evaluation specialists, and technical staff with varying levels of modelling experience.

title: Facilitator Guidance
text:
NoteFacilitation Principle



A well-prepared facilitator focuses not only on what will be taught, but also on how participants will engage with, discuss, and apply the material within their own programme contexts.



Preparation Checklist







Area
Key Considerations


Content
Review learning objectives, activities, and expected outputs


Participants
Understand backgrounds, roles, and country contexts


Materials
Prepare slides, worksheets, case studies, and supporting resources


Technology
Test virtual platforms, breakout rooms, polling tools, and presentations


Coordination
Align expectations with guest speakers and co-facilitators


Application
Identify links between module content and capstone projects





Creating an Effective Learning Environment
The Fellowship is most successful when participants feel comfortable contributing their experiences, questioning assumptions, and engaging with diverse perspectives. Facilitators should establish a learning environment that is respectful, participatory, and grounded in practical application. This is particularly important in a cohort that brings together participants with different professional roles, levels of technical experience, and country contexts.
An effective learning environment does not require all participants to have the same level of modelling knowledge. Instead, it should support shared learning across different forms of expertise. Programme managers, policymakers, surveillance officers, data analysts, and technical specialists each bring valuable perspectives. Facilitators should actively reinforce the idea that modelling for decision-making depends on combining technical insight with operational knowledge and policy judgement.






NoteCollaborative Learning Space



The Fellowship should feel like a collaborative learning space rather than a classroom. Participants should be encouraged to test ideas, raise concerns, and connect modelling concepts to real programme decisions.


Facilitators can support an effective learning environment by setting expectations early. At the start of the Fellowship, it is helpful to agree on shared norms for participation, discussion, and collaboration. These norms should emphasise respectful dialogue, curiosity, constructive challenge, and openness to different perspectives. Participants should also be reassured that uncertainty, disagreement, and incomplete information are normal features of modelling and public health decision-making.







Dimension
Facilitator Role


Psychological safety
Create space for participants to ask questions without fear of judgement


Participation
Encourage contributions from both technical and non-technical participants


Relevance
Link discussions to real malaria programme and policy challenges


Respect
Acknowledge different forms of expertise and country experience


Reflection
Build in time for participants to connect learning to their own roles


Collaboration
Support peer learning within and across country teams



Facilitators should pay close attention to the balance of voices in the room. Participants with technical backgrounds may be more comfortable discussing modelling concepts, while those in policy or programme roles may initially be less confident engaging with technical material. Conversely, technical participants may need support in thinking beyond model outputs towards operational feasibility, communication, and decision-making processes. The facilitator’s role is to help bridge these perspectives.
A useful approach is to invite participants to speak from their own experience before introducing more technical framing. For example, before discussing model assumptions, facilitators might ask participants how uncertainty appears in their programme planning work. Before introducing scenario analysis, facilitators might ask what kinds of strategic choices their programmes currently face. This helps participants recognise that many modelling concepts connect directly to decisions they already make.
Facilitators should also make deliberate use of peer learning. Participants often learn as much from one another as from formal presentations. Country examples, practical challenges, and programme experiences should be treated as core learning resources. Where possible, facilitators should invite participants to compare experiences across settings and reflect on how differences in transmission, health systems, data availability, funding, or governance affect the use of modelling.






TipFacilitator Tip



When a discussion becomes overly technical, ask: “What does this mean for a programme decision?” When a discussion becomes overly operational, ask: “What evidence or analysis would help clarify this decision?”


The learning environment should also support constructive challenge. Participants should feel able to question assumptions, critique model outputs, and identify limitations without dismissing the value of modelling. Facilitators can model this balance by using language such as “What would we need to know to interpret this result?” or “What assumptions would decision-makers need to understand?” rather than framing critique as right or wrong.
Finally, facilitators should create moments for synthesis. After exercises, group work, or discussion, time should be set aside to identify key insights, unresolved questions, and implications for participants’ own work. This helps ensure that learning does not remain abstract but is translated into practical understanding.







Practice
Example Facilitation Prompt


Connect to experience
Where have you seen this issue arise in your programme?


Encourage reflection
What assumption is most important for decision-makers to understand?


Bridge perspectives
How might a modeller and a programme manager view this differently?


Support application
How could this be used in strategic planning or resource allocation?


Promote synthesis
What is the main takeaway for policy or programme decision-making?



Creating an effective learning environment is an ongoing process throughout the Fellowship. Facilitators should regularly observe participation patterns, adapt activities where needed, and create opportunities for participants to engage in different ways, including plenary discussion, small group work, written reflection, and country team collaboration.

Time Management Considerations
Facilitators should prioritise discussion, reflection, and application over content coverage. Participants often gain more value from exploring one concept deeply than from rapidly progressing through multiple topics. Time should be protected for participant discussion, synthesis of key messages, and connections to programme realities.






CautionPractical reflections from delivering the inaugural cohort



While we did our best to stick to time and follow the schedule, we found that some sessions ran over time and others finished early. We recommend that facilitators build in flexibility to adapt timing based on participant engagement and discussion.
Further, during the intensive week blocks, we finished by 15.30 each day to allow time for fellows to address their regular work commitments. By intentionally setting aside this time, we had a more engagement throughout the day where fellows did not feel they needed to juggle attendance and ongoing work.

text:
Tips for Interactive and Adult Learning Approaches
The Fellowship is grounded in adult learning principles. Participants bring significant professional experience and practical knowledge, and the role of the facilitator is to create opportunities for participants to connect this experience with new concepts and approaches.

Adult Learning in Practice
Rather than positioning participants as recipients of knowledge, facilitators should encourage active engagement with real-world challenges. Learning is most effective when participants can see a clear connection between Fellowship content and decisions they face in their own programmes.

title: Facilitator Guidance
text:
Managing Group Work and Discussions
Group work is central to the Fellowship learning experience. Facilitators should focus on creating conditions that support meaningful participation, balanced discussion, and practical problem-solving.

Supporting Effective Participation
Clear instructions, realistic timeframes, and well-defined outputs are essential. Participants should understand what they are being asked to produce and why the activity is important.


Encouraging Balanced Contributions
In every cohort, some participants will be more comfortable speaking than others. Facilitators should create opportunities for all voices to be heard and should actively encourage contributions from quieter participants.


Facilitation Approaches







Effective Practice
Common Pitfall


Invite diverse perspectives
Allow one or two voices to dominate


Use structured discussion rounds
Assume silence indicates agreement


Break large groups into smaller teams

Summarise key insights regularly

Link activities to programme realities

ImportantKey Takeaway



Strong group discussions are characterised by participation, curiosity, and reflection. The facilitator’s role is to create the conditions for these qualities to emerge.

title: Facilitator Guidance
text:
Facilitating Technical–Policy Dialogue
A distinguishing feature of the RMMT Fellowship is its focus on bridging the gap between technical modelling and policy decision-making. Facilitators play a key role in helping participants navigate this interface.

Understanding Different Perspectives
Technical experts and decision-makers often approach problems differently. Technical participants may focus on assumptions, methods, and analytical rigour, while policymakers and programme managers are more likely to focus on feasibility, implementation, and strategic priorities.
Effective facilitation helps participants recognise that these perspectives are complementary rather than competing.


Translating Between Technical and Policy Language
Facilitators should consistently encourage participants to move beyond technical outputs and focus on their implications.
Questions that support this translation include:







Technical Question
Policy-Oriented Question


What does the model estimate?
What decision could this inform?


What assumptions were made?
What do decision-makers need to understand?


How robust are the findings?
How much confidence should we place in the recommendation?


What uncertainties remain?
What risks should be considered?





Managing Uncertainty
Uncertainty is a normal and expected feature of modelling and decision-making. Facilitators should help participants understand that uncertainty does not diminish the value of evidence. Instead, it provides important information about confidence, risk, and possible future outcomes.






NoteKey Takeaway



The purpose of modelling is not to predict the future with certainty, but to support better-informed decisions in situations where uncertainty exists.




Linking Dialogue to Capstone Projects
Capstone projects provide an opportunity for participants to practise technical–policy engagement in a realistic setting. Facilitators should encourage teams to think carefully about how questions are framed, how findings would be communicated, and how outputs could ultimately support decision-making processes.

title: Facilitator Guidance
text:
Facilitator Reflection and Continuous Improvement
Effective facilitation requires ongoing reflection and adaptation. Facilitators should regularly review participant engagement, learning outcomes, and feedback to identify opportunities for improvement.

Reflection Questions for Facilitators






TipReflection Questions for Facilitators



After each session, consider:

What generated the greatest engagement?
Which concepts proved most challenging?
Were learning objectives achieved?
How effectively were discussions linked to programme realities?
What should be adapted for future delivery?





Using Feedback for Improvement
Participant feedback should be viewed as a valuable source of information rather than simply a reporting requirement. Reviewing feedback regularly can help facilitators refine activities, strengthen discussions, improve examples, and ensure that future cohorts continue to find the Fellowship relevant, practical, and impactful.

title: Cross-Cutting Skills
text:
Communicating with Policymakers
Effective communication is central to policy-focused modelling. Modelling outputs rarely speak for themselves; they need to be translated into clear, relevant, and actionable messages that respond to the needs of decision-makers. Fellows should be encouraged to think not only about what the model shows, but also about what the intended audience needs to understand in order to use the evidence appropriately.
Policymakers and programme leaders often work under time pressure, with competing priorities and incomplete information. Communication should therefore focus on the decision being informed, the main findings, the level of confidence in those findings, and the implications for policy or programme action. Technical detail remains important, but it should be presented in a way that supports understanding rather than overwhelming the audience.
When communicating modelling results, fellows should aim to make messages concise, transparent, and relevant. This includes explaining assumptions, uncertainty, and limitations in accessible language. Rather than avoiding uncertainty, fellows should frame it as part of responsible decision-making.
A useful approach is to structure communication around a simple storyline: the problem, the evidence, the implications, and the recommended next steps. Visualisations, policy briefs, slide decks, and verbal presentations should all be designed with this storyline in mind.

title: Cross-Cutting Skills
text:
NoteCommunication Principle



Policy communication should begin with the decision context, not the model. The most important question is not “What did the model produce?” but “What decision can this evidence help inform?”











Communication Focus
Guiding Question



Decision relevance
What policy or programme decision does this evidence support?



Main finding
What is the key result or message decision-makers need to understand?



Assumptions
What assumptions shape the interpretation of the results?


Uncertainty
How confident should decision-makers be in the findings?


Implications
What are the practical options, risks, or trade-offs?


Action
What should be considered next?










TipFacilitator Prompt



Ask fellows to summarise a modelling result in three ways: first for a technical modeller, then for a malaria programme manager, and finally for a senior policymaker with limited time. This helps fellows practise adapting language, emphasis, and level of detail.

title: Cross-Cutting Skills
text:
Bridging Modelling and Decision-Making
Policy-focused modelling sits at the interface between technical analysis and real-world decision-making. Bridging these two domains requires more than technical accuracy. It requires a clear understanding of programme priorities, operational constraints, stakeholder needs, timelines, and the decisions that modelling evidence is intended to support.
Fellows should be encouraged to view modelling as a collaborative process. A model is most useful when the policy question is clearly defined, when assumptions are discussed openly, and when outputs are interpreted with programme context in mind. This means engaging decision-makers and technical partners early, rather than presenting modelling results only at the end of an analysis.






NoteBridging Principle



Modelling is most policy-relevant when decision-makers and technical experts work together to define the question, interpret the results, and identify feasible actions.


The bridge between modelling and decision-making can be strengthened by focusing on the full evidence-use pathway: from question formulation to analysis, interpretation, communication, and action. Each step requires dialogue between those producing evidence and those responsible for using it.








Step
Policy-Focused Consideration



Define the question
Is the modelling question linked to a real decision or programme priority?



Clarify assumptions
Are key assumptions transparent and understandable to non-technical stakeholders?



Generate outputs
Are outputs presented in formats that support comparison and interpretation?



Interpret findings
What do the findings mean in light of programme realities, constraints, and uncertainty?



Communicate evidence
Are results communicated clearly for the intended audience?


Support action
What decisions, discussions, or next steps could the evidence inform?




Fellows should also consider timing. Even high-quality modelling may have limited influence if results are delivered after key planning or budgeting decisions have already been made. Policy-focused modelling therefore requires awareness of strategic planning cycles, funding windows, review meetings, and other decision points.






ImportantTiming Matters



For modelling evidence to influence policy, it must be available when decisions are being discussed. Fellows should consider policy and programme timelines early in the modelling process.

title: Cross-Cutting Skills
text:
Facilitating Technical–Policy Dialogue
Technical–policy dialogue is the process of bringing together modelling experts, programme teams, policymakers, and other stakeholders to jointly understand evidence and its implications. Effective dialogue helps ensure that modelling questions are relevant, outputs are interpreted appropriately, and recommendations are grounded in programme realities.
Facilitators play an important role in creating a space where different types of expertise are valued. Modellers may bring knowledge of methods, assumptions, data, and uncertainty, while programme teams and policymakers bring knowledge of implementation, feasibility, political context, resource constraints, and strategic priorities. Productive dialogue depends on recognising that all of these perspectives are necessary.






NoteDialogue Principle



Technical–policy dialogue is not simply about explaining models to policymakers. It is about creating shared understanding between people with different expertise, responsibilities, and decision-making needs.


Fellows should learn to facilitate dialogue by asking questions that connect technical outputs to programme decisions. These questions can help move discussions from abstract model results to practical interpretation and action.







Technical Framing
Policy-Focused Reframing


What does the model estimate?
What decision could this estimate help inform?


What assumptions were used?
Which assumptions are most important for decision-makers to understand?


How uncertain are the results?
What risks or trade-offs should be considered?


Which scenario performs best?
Which option is most feasible, affordable, and aligned with programme priorities?


What additional data are needed?
What decisions can be made now, and what evidence should be strengthened over time?



Good facilitation also involves managing power dynamics and participation. Some stakeholders may be more confident with technical language, while others may be more familiar with policy or implementation realities. Facilitators should ensure that no single perspective dominates and that technical uncertainty does not prevent constructive discussion.






TipFacilitator Prompt



When discussion becomes too technical, ask: “What does this mean for a programme decision?” When discussion becomes too broad, ask: “What evidence would help clarify this choice?”


Technical–policy dialogue should end with synthesis. Participants should be clear on what was discussed, what evidence suggests, what uncertainties remain, and what actions or next steps are needed.

title: Cross-Cutting Skills
section: Using Evidence for Advocacy and Resource Mobilisation
text:
Using Evidence for Advocacy and Resource Mobilisation
Modelling evidence can play an important role in advocacy and resource mobilisation by helping programmes describe the potential consequences of action, inaction, or alternative investment choices. When used appropriately, modelling can support a clearer case for funding, prioritisation, and strategic decision-making.
Advocacy-focused use of modelling should remain transparent and responsible. The aim is not to overstate certainty or present modelling as proof of a single correct decision. Instead, modelling evidence should help stakeholders understand possible futures, compare options, and assess the likely implications of different choices.






NoteAdvocacy Principle



Modelling evidence is most useful for advocacy when it connects investment choices to plausible programme outcomes, while clearly explaining assumptions, uncertainty, and limitations.


Fellows should be encouraged to identify the audience and purpose of advocacy before selecting messages or outputs. A Ministry of Health audience may need evidence on programme priorities and feasibility, while a financing partner may need information on expected impact, value for money, or risks of underinvestment.







Advocacy Question
How Modelling Evidence Can Help


Why is action needed?
Show projected disease burden, risks, or consequences of delayed action


Which option should be prioritised?
Compare intervention scenarios, target populations, or implementation strategies


What is the expected impact?
Estimate potential cases, deaths, infections, or other outcomes averted


What resources are required?
Link intervention options to costs, feasibility, and expected benefits


What are the trade-offs?
Compare alternative uses of limited resources


What is the risk of inaction?
Illustrate potential future scenarios if current gaps remain unaddressed



Evidence used for advocacy should be tailored to the audience. This may involve preparing a short policy brief, a focused slide deck, a one-page summary, or a set of figures that clearly compare scenarios. Messages should be simple enough to support decision-making, while retaining enough transparency to avoid misinterpretation.






ImportantResponsible Advocacy



Advocacy messages should not hide uncertainty. Clear communication of uncertainty can strengthen credibility by showing that recommendations are based on careful interpretation rather than overconfidence.


Resource mobilisation also benefits from combining modelling evidence with other forms of evidence. Cost data, implementation experience, equity considerations, feasibility assessments, and stakeholder priorities should all be considered alongside modelled estimates of impact.
By strengthening these cross-cutting skills, fellows will be better equipped to support the responsible use of modelling evidence in malaria policy, planning, advocacy, and investment discussions.

title: MEL Framework
text:
Approach to Monitoring and Evaluation
The Monitoring and Evaluation (M&E) approach for the RMMT Fellowship is designed to assess how fellows’ competencies, confidence, and perceptions change over the course of the programme. Rather than treating evaluation as a one-off reporting activity, the Fellowship uses M&E as a learning mechanism: to understand participant progress, identify areas where additional support is needed, and inform improvements to future delivery.
The M&E framework is structured around three assessment points: baseline, midline, and endline. Each phase serves a distinct purpose.
The baseline survey should be administered before or at the start of the Fellowship. It establishes fellows’ initial confidence, prior exposure to modelling, expectations for the programme, and perceived learning needs. This information can help facilitators understand the cohort and adapt early sessions to participants’ backgrounds.
The midline survey should be administered approximately halfway through the Fellowship. Its primary purpose is formative. It should help facilitators understand what is working well, which topics require additional explanation, and whether fellows feel supported in applying learning to their capstone projects. Midline findings should be reviewed quickly so that practical adjustments can be made during the Fellowship.
The endline survey should be administered at the end of the Fellowship. It assesses perceived changes in competency, satisfaction with programme delivery, and fellows’ intentions to use modelling evidence in their work. It should also capture reflections on the Fellowship structure, module sequencing, capstone process, and suggestions for future cohorts.
A mixed-methods approach is used, combining quantitative competency assessment with qualitative feedback. Quantitative data are collected through a 14-item Likert scale covering key competency areas. Qualitative data are collected through open-ended questions and interactive feedback activities, allowing fellows to explain their experiences, identify barriers, and suggest improvements. Together, these methods identify how the Fellowship can better support fellows to apply modelling evidence in real programme and policy contexts.

title: MEL Framework
text:
M&E Phase
Primary Purpose



Baseline
Establish fellows’ starting confidence, expectations, and self-assessed competencies



Midline
Identify emerging learning needs, implementation issues, and opportunities to adapt delivery


Endline
Assess perceived learning gains, satisfaction, and intended application of Fellowship learning












NoteFormative Use of Feedback



The midline survey is especially important because it allows the delivery team to respond while the Fellowship is still underway. Findings should be reviewed promptly and translated into practical adjustments where possible.









NotePurpose of M&E



The purpose of M&E is not only to measure whether learning occurred, but also to understand how the Fellowship can better support fellows to apply modelling evidence in real programme and policy contexts.

title: MEL Framework
text:
Competency Assessment Tool
The suggested quantitative competency assessment tool is comprised of 14 closed questions using a five-point Likert scale. The scale is scored from 1 to 5, where 1 = Strongly Disagree, 2 = Disagree, 3 = Neutral, 4 = Agree, and 5 = Strongly Agree. These questions remain consistent across the baseline, midline, and endline surveys to support comparison over time.
The questions are grouped into three competency areas: understanding and interpreting modelling outputs; applying modelling to decision-making; and collaboration, communication, and influence. These areas reflect the Fellowship’s emphasis on both technical understanding and the practical use of modelling evidence in policy and programme settings.
The open-ended questions vary across surveys. At baseline, they focus on expectations, prior experience, and anticipated learning needs. At midline, they focus on what is working well, where fellows require further support, and how delivery could be improved. At endline, they focus on learning gains, application, and recommendations for future cohorts.






TipInterpreting Competency Scores



The competency assessment is based on self-reported confidence and perceived ability. Scores should therefore be interpreted as indicators of perceived progress rather than as direct tests of technical proficiency.

title: MEL Framework
section: Guidance on Data Collection and Analysis
text:
Guidance on Data Collection and Analysis
Data collection should be planned in advance and integrated into the Fellowship delivery schedule. Surveys should be short enough to encourage completion, but detailed enough to capture meaningful information. Participants should be given clear instructions on the purpose of each survey, how the data will be used, and whether responses will be anonymous or identifiable.
Where possible, surveys should be administered using a consistent platform across all three evaluation points. This helps ensure that responses are comparable over time and simplifies data management. Fellows should be reminded that honest feedback is valuable and that both positive and critical responses will be used to strengthen the Fellowship.
Quantitative analysis should focus on changes in self-assessed competency scores over time. For each competency area, the analysis may include mean scores at baseline, midline, and endline, as well as changes between assessment points. These summaries can help identify areas where fellows report the strongest gains and areas where further support may be needed.
Qualitative analysis should focus on recurring themes in open-ended responses. Responses can be grouped into categories such as useful content, challenging topics, delivery feedback, capstone support needs, and anticipated application. Short illustrative quotes may be used in reporting, provided confidentiality is protected.






ImportantData Interpretation



Changes in Likert scores should be interpreted alongside qualitative feedback. A numerical increase may indicate improved confidence, but open-ended responses help explain why change occurred and what additional support fellows may still need.


When reporting findings, results should be presented in a way that is clear and actionable. Long tables of scores may be useful for internal analysis, but programme teams and facilitators may benefit more from short summaries that identify key trends, priority areas for improvement, and practical recommendations.

title: MEL Framework
section: Using Feedback to Adapt and Improve Delivery
text:
Using Feedback to Adapt and Improve Delivery
Feedback should be treated as an active part of Fellowship delivery rather than as a final reporting requirement. The M&E process should create structured opportunities for the delivery team to reflect on what is working, respond to fellows’ needs, and improve the curriculum over time.
Midline feedback is particularly useful for real-time adaptation. For example, if fellows report low confidence in interpreting uncertainty, facilitators may choose to revisit this topic in a later session, provide an additional worked example, or create more time for discussion during capstone support sessions. If fellows report that exercises are too technical or not sufficiently connected to programme realities, facilitators can adjust examples, prompts, and group work to strengthen relevance.
Endline feedback should be used to inform future cohorts. This may include revising module sequencing, strengthening pre-reading materials, adapting facilitation approaches, adjusting the balance between technical inputs and discussion, or improving support for capstone projects.







Feedback Finding
Possible Adaptation


Fellows want more technical support
Add worked examples, optional technical refreshers, or additional office hours


Fellows need clearer capstone guidance
Strengthen links between module content and capstone milestones


Fellows find content too abstract
Use more country examples, applied scenarios, and programme-relevant discussion prompts


Fellows report low confidence
Add structured peer discussion, facilitator check-ins, and additional reflection activities


Fellows request more interaction
Increase time for breakout discussions, country team work, and plenary synthesis



A strong M&E approach should therefore support both accountability and learning. It should document the value of the Fellowship while also providing timely information that helps facilitators, partners, and future cohorts improve the experience and strengthen the use of modelling evidence in malaria decision-making.

title: Competency Assessment Tool
text:
Quantitative Component
The quantitative component of the competency assessment tool is designed to track changes in fellows’ self-reported confidence, understanding, and ability to use modelling evidence over the course of the Fellowship. The same 14 Likert-scale questions are used at baseline, midline, and endline, allowing responses to be compared across time points.
The questions are organised around three competency areas that reflect the core aims of the RMMT Fellowship: understanding and interpreting modelling outputs; applying modelling to decision-making; and collaboration, communication, and influence. Together, these areas capture both technical engagement with modelling and the broader skills required to translate modelling evidence into policy-relevant action.
Each question is scored on a five-point Likert scale, where 1 = Strongly Disagree and 5 = Strongly Agree. Scores can be analysed by individual question, competency area, survey time point, and cohort. Changes in scores over time should be interpreted as changes in fellows’ perceived confidence and capability, rather than as a formal test of technical proficiency.

title: Competency Assessment Tool
text:
Qualitative Component
The qualitative component is designed to provide richer insight into fellows’ experiences, learning needs, and reflections on the Fellowship. While the quantitative questions allow change to be tracked across time, the open-ended questions help explain how and why that change occurs.
The qualitative questions vary across baseline, midline, and endline surveys to reflect the different purpose of each evaluation point. At baseline, questions focus on expectations, prior experience, and areas where fellows feel least confident. At midline, questions focus on progress, challenges, and support needs while there is still time to adapt delivery. At endline, questions explore overall experience, perceived learning gains, programme design, broader impact, and future application.
This component is particularly important for understanding how fellows connect the curriculum to their own roles, country contexts, capstone projects, and policy environments. Responses can help identify which aspects of the Fellowship are most useful, which topics require additional support, and how future cohorts could be strengthened.






TipUsing Qualitative Feedback



Open-ended feedback should be reviewed during the Fellowship, not only at the end. Midline responses are especially valuable because they allow facilitators to adjust pacing, revisit challenging topics, provide additional examples, or strengthen capstone support while the programme is still underway.

title: Glossary
text:
Glossary of Key Modelling Terms
This glossary provides definitions for key modelling and evaluation terms used throughout the Fellowship curriculum. It is intended to support a shared understanding of technical language across fellows, facilitators, programme teams, and policy stakeholders.

The glossary has been adapted from the World Health Organization (2026) publication Guidance for using modelling for immunization decision-making. Where useful, definitions have been lightly edited for readability and relevance to the RMMT Fellowship context.








Term
Definition


Assumption
An input or condition taken as true for modelling purposes, which may not fully reflect real-life complexity.


Benefit–cost ratio
The ratio of benefits to costs. This metric is commonly used in benefit–cost analysis to evaluate two or more policy options, interventions, or programmes in terms of their costs and outcomes in monetary terms.


Case fatality ratio
The ratio of the number of deaths from a disease to the number of cases of the disease.


Counterfactual
A scenario representing what has not happened or would not happen.


Cross-validation / Cross-validity
A type of model comparison that can be used during model validation. It consists of testing a model on data excluded from the dataset. This may involve the same model with different subsets of data, or different sets of parameters.


Deterministic
A type of model in which the outcome is determined only by the inputs and not by randomness.


External validity
A type of model comparison that can be used during model validation. It consists of comparing model results with the real world.


Face validity
A type of model comparison that can be used during model validation. It consists of conferring with field experts to evaluate model structure, data sources, assumptions, and results.


Incremental cost-effectiveness ratio
A metric used in cost–utility analysis to compare two policy options, interventions, or programmes. It is calculated as the difference in costs divided by the difference in health outcomes between the interventions or programmes. The ratio represents the additional cost required to gain one additional unit of health benefit, such as a life-year gained or a disability-adjusted life-year averted.


Internal validity
A type of model comparison that can be used during model validation. It consists of checking the accuracy of coding and data analyses.


Mathematical model
A representation of a real-world system using mathematical concepts, including equations or formulas.


Model fitting / Model fit
The process of adjusting the parameters of a model so its outputs closely match, or are calibrated to, observed data. This ensures the model accurately represents historical or current conditions before being used for projections or scenario analyses.


Model validation
The process of assessing whether a model accurately predicts data that were not used during model fitting. It involves testing the reliability and credibility of the model in different contexts or time periods.


Multimodel comparison
A type of model cross-validation that involves comparing the outputs of different models that address the same question or scenario. This can help identify consistent findings, understand uncertainties, and assess how differences in model structure or assumptions influence results.


Parameter
A value used to represent a property in a model, such as the rate at which people with an infection recover. When a parameter is adjusted, the model’s result will change.


Predictive validity
A measure of how well a model performs in predicting the occurrence of actual empirically observed outcomes.


Projection
An estimate of what could happen in the future, based on model assumptions.


Scenario
A specific set of assumptions used in the model to estimate what might happen under certain conditions, such as different levels of vaccine coverage or target age groups.


Sensitivity analysis
Testing how results change when assumptions or inputs are varied to check the robustness of findings.


SIR model
A model in which the population is divided into people who are susceptible, infected, or removed/recovered. People in the population move between these different states.


Stochastic
A model that will produce a different output, or result, each time it is run, introducing randomness.


Uncertainty
The degree to which model results might vary because of incomplete knowledge or variability in data.
